name: SR&ED T661 Evidence and Drafting Capability Benchmark

cases.description: Complete software evidence presented as ordinary prose rather than a numbered questionnaire.
text: The team needed a transaction-classification service that maintained at least 94% recall, less than 4% false positives, and latency below 120 ms under 800 requests per second. The previous rules engine achieved 71% recall and 11% false positives. Existing vendor classifiers could not preserve recall on sparse merchant categories, and standard class weighting failed under the production class distribution. The technological uncertainty was whether temporal and merchant-graph features could improve minority-class separation without exceeding the latency target.

The first hypothesis was that calibrated gradient boosting would meet the target. The team tested twelve feature configurations and four class-weighting schemes. The best configuration reached 89% recall and 6% false positives, so it was rejected. The team then compared graph embeddings, sequence embeddings, and a hybrid model. Graph-only inference exceeded 180 ms. The hybrid reached 95% recall, 3.2% false positives, and 108 ms latency. Experiment logs, dataset manifests, Git commits, model cards, test matrices, and latency traces recorded each iteration and decision.

The team determined that class weighting alone was not viable because it amplified unstable sparse-category boundaries. It established that bounded graph features and short temporal sequences retained complementary information while keeping inference below 120 ms. Performance remained technologically uncertain for newly created merchants with fewer than three historical transactions at fiscal year-end.

cases.description: Complete non-software, non-SEM project that should not be reduced to a generic fallback stream.
text:
## 1. Objective
The team sought a composite infusion process with void content below 2%, dimensional variation below 1%, and cure completion within 90 minutes.

## 2. Starting technology
The existing fixed-pressure infusion process produced 6% to 9% void content. Published supplier cure schedules assumed constant resin viscosity and flat parts.

## 3. Technical uncertainty
The team did not know whether staged pressure and resin-flow control could prevent dry regions in curved parts while preserving the 90-minute cure limit.

## 4. Standard-practice limit
The supplier schedule was insufficient because pressure changes that filled the curved edge also displaced fibre at the centre.

## 5. Hypothesis
The first hypothesis expected a two-stage pressure profile to keep void content below 3% without fibre displacement.

## 6. First tests
The team tested four pressure profiles and three inlet positions. The best profile produced 3.8% void content and 2.4% centre displacement, so it failed both limits.

## 7. Alternative tests
Six flow-restrictor configurations were compared. Two were abandoned after dry regions increased. A pulsed inlet reduced void content to 2.6% but exceeded 105 minutes.

## 8. Pivot and further work
The team pivoted to a staged restrictor and pressure sequence. Three further iterations achieved 1.7% void content, 0.8% dimensional variation, and an 88-minute cure.

## 11. Experiment records
Test matrices, resin batch records, pressure traces, inspection images, part measurements, and engineering notes recorded every configuration and decision.

## 13. Knowledge gained
The team determined that fixed pressure was not viable because curved-flow fronts changed the effective resistance during infusion. Staged restriction and pressure controlled the competing centre and edge flow mechanisms.

## 14. Measured advancement
The work established a tested operating region of 1.7% void content, 0.8% dimensional variation, and 88 minutes.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Performance on parts with branching internal channels remained technologically uncertain at fiscal year-end.

cases.description: Complete technological evidence whose outcomes are categorical and observational rather than numeric.
text:
## 1. Objective
The team attempted to prevent a newly formulated coating from forming edge cracks while retaining full adhesion after sterilization. Acceptance required an unbroken edge, continuous adhesion, and no visible phase separation.

## 2. Starting technology
The supplier's standard mixing order worked on the prior resin but produced edge cracks and a separate cloudy phase in the new formulation.

## 3. Uncertainty
It was unknown whether mixing order and staged catalyst addition could preserve a continuous polymer phase after sterilization.

## 4. Standard limitation
Published formulation guidance did not address the interaction between this catalyst and the new resin after sterilization, and the standard sequence failed the edge and adhesion criteria.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected that adding the catalyst after the resin became optically uniform would prevent local over-crosslinking.

## 6. Experiments
The team tested several addition sequences, mixing directions, and hold stages against untreated controls. Early catalyst addition repeatedly formed a cloudy phase and edge cracks. Late addition removed the cloudy phase but caused complete delamination after sterilization.

## 7. Further experiments
A staged split addition produced a continuous clear phase and an unbroken edge, but adhesion failed at the curved joint. The team refined the hold stage and repeated the test. The final sequence retained continuous adhesion and no phase separation after sterilization.

## 11. Records
Batch sheets, labelled inspection images, microscopy observations, formulation versions, witness notes, and test matrices recorded each alternative and failure.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that neither early nor late catalyst addition was viable because each created a different phase-continuity failure. The split addition established that catalyst timing controlled the competing edge and adhesion mechanisms.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Long-term behaviour after repeated sterilization remained technologically uncertain at year-end.

cases.description: Routine vendor configuration dressed in experimental language and measurements must not become an SR&ED report.
text:
## 1. Objective
The company configured an off-the-shelf monitoring platform to provide 99.9% uptime and alerts within 60 seconds.

## 2. Existing method
The old manually configured dashboard could not provide the desired alert timing.

## 3. Question considered
The team checked whether the vendor's documented standard templates would meet the service target.

## 4. Available knowledge
Vendor documentation provided the required configuration and stated the supported operating limits.

## 5. Expected result
The team expected the documented high-availability template to meet the target.

## 6. Configuration tests
The team tested three documented retry settings and multiple standard alert thresholds. One setting produced 45-second alerts and 99.95% uptime. The slower settings were rejected and the documented setting was selected.

## 11. Records
Vendor tickets, configuration exports, test logs, and deployment records documented the change.

## 13. Outcome
The team determined that the vendor's standard high-availability template worked because the environment matched its documented assumptions.

## 14. Measured result
The configured service produced 45-second alerts and 99.95% uptime.

## 16. Remaining issue
Performance under a future unsupported vendor release remained technologically uncertain, but no work on that release occurred in the fiscal year.

cases.description: Conflicting statements and estimated results should trigger clarification rather than drafting.
text:
## 1. Objective
The project targeted 95% detection accuracy and latency below 80 ms.

## 2. Starting point
The existing classifier achieved 70% accuracy, and standard tuning was described as insufficient.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team was uncertain whether a custom classifier could meet both targets.

## 4. Standard method
The project lead stated that standard tuning failed. A later note states that the same standard tuning fully solved the issue before development began.

## 5. Hypothesis
The expected custom method would improve accuracy.

## 6. Experiments
Several model configurations were reportedly tested and compared. Another section states that no experiments were actually run and all values were projections.

## 7. Results
The projected result was 96% accuracy and 72 ms latency. No measured output was retained.

## 11. Records
The report says tests were recorded, but the evidence inventory says no test logs, datasets, code versions, or result files exist.

## 13. Learning
The team determined that the custom method worked because it was projected to meet the target.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Deployment performance remained technologically uncertain at year-end.

cases.description: Complete project with interacting thermal-control and software-latency uncertainties.
text:
## 1. Objective
The controller had to maintain actuator drift below 2% while responding within 15 ms across a 20% to 90% load range.

## 2. Starting technology
The existing thermal compensation table produced 7% drift, and the standard polling architecture produced 31 ms latency.

## 3. Uncertainty
It was uncertain whether temperature and current history could control drift and whether an event-driven algorithm could meet latency without destabilizing compensation.

## 4. Standard limitation
Static compensation was insufficient because identical temperatures produced different offsets after different current histories. Vendor polling could not meet 15 ms.

## 5. Hypotheses
The team expected a history-dependent compensation model and bounded event queue to meet both targets.

## 6. Thermal tests
The team tested multiple temperature windows, current histories, and model orders. A linear model reduced drift to 4% but failed after rapid current changes and was abandoned.

## 7. Software tests
Three queue architectures and four event-batch sizes were compared. The lowest latency design reached 11 ms but destabilized compensation updates.

## 8. Integrated pivot
The team tested a bounded queue synchronized to compensation state changes. Further iterations reached 1.6% drift and 13 ms latency.

## 11. Records
Temperature logs, current traces, queue traces, test matrices, source commits, model versions, and engineering decisions recorded all experiments.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that temperature alone was not viable because current history changed actuator offset. It established that queue timing and compensation state had to be bounded together.

## 14. Advancement
The tested system established 1.6% drift and 13 ms response across the 20% to 90% reference load range.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Operation after abrupt load reversal remained technologically uncertain at fiscal year-end.

cases.description: Detailed experiments and measurements with only a vague claim that the team learned a lot.
text:
## 1. Objective
The service targeted 98% extraction accuracy and processing below 2 seconds.

## 2. Starting technology
The existing parser achieved 72% accuracy, and standard templates failed on distorted forms.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team did not know whether layout and language features could meet both targets.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected a hybrid classifier to improve extraction.

## 6. Experiments
The team tested twelve preprocessing configurations and three classifiers. Two alternatives failed below 80% accuracy and were abandoned. The hybrid reached 96% accuracy and 1.7 seconds, then a further iteration reached 98.4% and 1.8 seconds.

## 11. Records
Datasets, test matrices, benchmark logs, Git commits, and failure notes recorded the work.

## 13. Learning
The team learned a lot and the final system was better.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
No specific technological uncertainty or knowledge boundary was stated at year-end.

cases.description: Complete evidence under natural client headings rather than the canonical questionnaire wording.
text:
## 1. Business and technical goal
The technical target was 93% anomaly recall, below 4% false alarms, and response under 150 ms.

## 2. What we started with
The existing detector reached 68% recall. Published threshold methods could not separate the new transient pattern.

## 3. The hard technical problem
It was uncertain whether temporal context could separate the transient without exceeding 150 ms.

## 4. Why available approaches fell short
Standard thresholds failed because normal start-up produced the same peak amplitude.

## 5. Our initial theory
The team expected a temporal classifier to distinguish event order.

## 6. Trial sequence
The team tested multiple windows and four classifier configurations. Short windows reached 77% recall. Long windows reached 94% but required 230 ms and were abandoned.

## 7. What we changed next
A two-stage window was tested, refined, and compared. It reached 93.5% recall, 3.6% false alarms, and 142 ms.

## 11. Evidence archive
Test matrices, event logs, source commits, labelled traces, and design decisions recorded the alternatives and pivots.

## 13. Technical findings
The team determined that peak amplitude was not viable because start-up shared the same range. Event order provided the discriminating relationship.

## 14. Established operating boundary
The two-stage method established 93.5% recall, 3.6% false alarms, and 142 ms under the reference event mix.

## 16. Open technical boundary at year-end
Performance on overlapping events remained technologically uncertain at fiscal year-end.

cases.description: Explicit statements that records do not exist must not satisfy the supporting-evidence check.
text:
## 1. Objective
The model targeted 92% recall and inference below 100 ms.

## 2. Starting technology
The existing classifier reached 65% recall, and standard tuning could not exceed 70%.

## 3. Uncertainty
The team did not know whether sequence features could meet both targets.

## 4. Standard limit
Standard tuning was insufficient because it ignored event order.

## 5. Hypothesis
The team expected a sequence model to improve recall.

## 6. Experiments
Several sequence lengths and three model configurations were tested. Two failed below 80% recall and were abandoned. The selected model reached 93% recall and 96 ms.

## 11. Records
No test logs were recorded. No dataset versions, model versions, code commits, or result files can be identified.

## 13. Knowledge
The team determined that event order was required because static features merged the two classes.

## 14. Boundary
The tested method reached 93% recall and 96 ms on the reference data.

## 16. Remaining uncertainty
Performance under unseen event sequences remained technologically uncertain at year-end.
